Author: @sokar_rostau
Content:
In the '90s, I worked at a cafe-bakery chain called Delifrance, which is apparently still huge in some countries but is mostly forgotten here in Australia. The chain's main thing is that the ovens and proover were behind the front counter so that customers could watch the bread and patisseries being cooked and get one straight from the oven if they wished. 

A customer and staff favourite on the winter-only menu was pumpkin soup served in a bowl made from a hollowed-out sourdough, about 1/3 the size of a regular one, with or without the 'sops'. As delicious as it was in a loaf that was 30 seconds out of the oven, the best part was that the soup would soak into the crusty walls of the bowl so that once it was gone you could tear apart the bowl for sops that were soaked on one side and still crusty on the other. There was probably a 50/50 split between customers who just ate the soup and left, and those that just left a few crumbs on the plate.

I would still call this the best soup I've ever had.

Author: @justridexc
Content: Love the soup, Max, but I'm a bit confused by your reference to the "Huron-Iroquois". Two different peoples.  The "Huron" (more correctly, the Wendat -- Huron was the name the French gave them, around the time they also gave them smallpox) and the "Iroquois" (more correctly, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, or Five Nations -- Mohawk, Seneca, Oneida, Onondaga, and Cayuga) both occupied what is now eastern Canada at the time of Cartier's visit/invasion, along with Anishinaabe peoples (aka "Ojibway" or "Algonquin" peoples, though there were three main groups, the Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatami).  Different groups, with different allegiances to the French and British colonizers who arrived in waves following Cartier and Champlain.  I'm a descendant of settlers myself, but I think it's important that we acknowledge indigenous peoples by the names they use themselves, not the appellations and corrupted versions we've been carelessly using for centuries.

Author: @birdgirl2623
Content: I make a savory pumpkin-spice soup by combining a can of pure pumpkin pulp and coconut milk (or cream of coconut--this is the stuff in the cans and should have NO sugar, and preferably not any weird additives, but it's getting harder to avoid added thickeners).  The spice is about a couple of tsp of garam masala powder (amount depends on strength of the spice mix--I get mine either from an Indian market or at this specialty spice store) .  Adjust thickness of soup with water. Adding about 1 tablespoon of virgin unrefined coconut oil can add to the richness and bumps up the coconut but this is optional (especially when using the thicker cream of coconut).  Salt to taste. I also add a touch of garlic powder, but that's also optional.  If you can't find (or make) garam masala (I think different regions and families have different mixes), don't substitute curry powder.  You might try to use pumpkin pie spice mix and add in some coriander and cardamon.  A lot of grocery store versions of "garam masala" is pretty much pumpkin pie spice mix with a higher price tag.  You just simmer the soup for maybe about 20 to 30 minutes just to let the flavors meld. Don't add sugar, the pumpkin and coconut milk has natural sweetness to it. Otherwise you're just eating heated up pumpkin pie filling or something.  I started to make this because I was trying to use up stuff in the cabinet.

Author: @racheljones9263
Content: Pumpkin soup is my absolute favorite food and I make it every year. I like a roasted pumpkin soup more than what’s made in the video and this the recipe I always use, I know it by heart and don’t use measurements anymore so this is my best approximation of what I do lol: get two pumpkin pie pumpkins and cut them in half, take out all the seeds and stringy bits. Put a light coating of olive oil on the flesh side and season generously with salt and pepper. Put the seasoned pumpkin halves face down on a baking sheet with aluminum foil and roast at 400 degrees Fahrenheit until fork tender, it usually takes about 45 ish minutes. Take them out to cool and once they are safe to touch peel off the skin. While the pumpkins are cooling get a pot and sauté one roughly chopped white onion until translucent. Towards the end of the onions cooking add minced garlic, as much as your heart desires which for me is usually 4-5 cloves. Once the onions are translucent and the garlic is aromatic add in the pealed roasted pumpkin and a 32oz container of broth, I prefer chicken but vegetable can also be used. While everything begins to heat up, begin blending with an immersion blender until smooth. Allow the soup to come to a simmer and adjust the thinness of the soup with broth to desired consistency. Then season to taste, I usually add some better than bouillon premium roast chicken base and white pepper. Finally top off with a generous splash of cream. Sorry for the long comment but I hope someone finds enjoyment from my favorite thing to eat!!!

Author: @michaelarmajo4572
Content:
As far as Native American history goes, corn, beans, and squash — including pumpkins — were known as the Three Sisters. These crops were grown together in a clever companion system: corn provided stalks for beans to climb, beans enriched the soil with nitrogen, and squash or pumpkins covered the ground, protecting roots and keeping the soil moist. This was ancient knowledge passed down for generations.

Interestingly, the pumpkins we use today in pies are New World pumpkins, different from the Old World ‘pumpion’ that Greeks and Romans cooked with — which were actually gourds or melons. It’s amazing to see how these traditions and plants traveled across time and continents. Now I’m just here cooking my pumpkin pie, carrying on that legacy in my own way!

Author: @rabbithorserunning
Content:
I cried when I saw Max wasting the seeds and the pulp!    If you don't like waste, you can cook the seeds for a snack AND use the pulp in the soup, too.  Be ready to get your hands messy:  using your fingers, separate all the seeds from the pulp & put the seeds in a strainer and the pulp in a separate bowl. Rinse the seeds really good and let them sit overnight to drain & dry, then toss them in a bit of olive oil & salt, then toast them in a skillet over medium heat, stirring constantly until they're tan & toasty (watch them carefully, as they can burn quick). Let them cool a bit, then MUNCH AWAY!  Crunchy snack!   

For the PULP:  once you've cleaned all the seeds out, put all the pulp into a blender & puree until smooth.  You can then mix that puree with the rest of the pumpkin for the soup, or use in your pies.

Content: Regarding the recipe calling for butter even during Lent: The medieval Catholic church would sell indulgences, or penances you could do ahead of time so your sin wouldn’t count, essentially. I think the theology is a little more complicated than that, but the upshot is that in France, an indulgence that allowed people to use butter during Lent became so popular that they were able to build a cathedral with the money raised from sales of said indulgence. So the recipe was probably written with the assumption that whoever was making it during Lent had purchased the butter indulgence, which is so stereotypically French that the joke writes itself.

Author: @KenJohnsonUSA
Content: I really wish Max hadn't conflated pumpkins with gourds so much. Gourds were from Africa and Asia. They could be dried for vessels, some were eaten in manner similar to cucumbers and eggplant, etc. Squash and pumpkin are entirely a New World plant.  For the Native Americans, there often was no delineation between squash and pumpkin. The word "squash " came from the Algonquin "a-skoo-te-squah-sh" which means "eaten when green." For the Aniyvwiya (Cherokee) we called all squash and pumpkins "iya." Pumpkins and squash were never dried because the shell is too brittle to be used like gourd. To say "New World pumpkin" is to imply that there was an Old World pumpkin...which there wasn't.  Did Native Americans use dried gourds for dippers and bowls? Yes...but we got them from the Europeans and Black slaves. The same is true for the bow and arrow...we got them from the Spanish.  😊

Author: @mwater_moon2865
Content:
There's a much easier way to prep a pumpkin and cook it.  I really recommend Jarrahdale if you can get one, VERY tasty and dark orange flesh but the outside is blue.  It's also REALLY hard, so trying to cut it to cubes is likely to take off a limb or at least a digit.
Wash your pumpkin (you can leave the stem if it's clean or remove it for ease of handling), and cut in half.  Remove seeds and strings (save for roasting the seeds if you so desire).  Place the cut sides down with skin still on in a large roasting pan with a lip (you need the lip to reduce mess) covered in foil or a silicon mat to help prevent sticking (you can oil the foil if you so desire but I don't bother with the silipad) and roast in a warm oven (about 325F) until the side dents if you push on it.  About the same give as a baked potato. The time varies greatly by the size of the pumpkin so check on it every 10 min or so after the first 20 min.
Now, take it out and let it cool, once you can handle it, just scrape the cooked pumpkin flesh out of the skin like you would an avocado. Viola, the prep time is about 10 minutes and even before I pureed with an immersion blender to skip all straining part, it was still very quick to pull out the few strings with a pair of electric beaters, the strings will wrap around the whisk parts.  
Since my pumpkins are very large I tend to portion it into zipper bags and freeze leftovers for the next year too.

Author: @ArthurEKing8472
Content:
While this is a perfectly fine method of preparing pumpkin puree, I tend to do something a little different.  (Obviously not 'historical' but hey...  It's entirely plausible they could have done it this way.)  My method IS MORE WORK!  However, in my experience (And I've done this almost every year for decades) you get SO MUCH MORE FLAVOUR this way.  And as pure pumpkin is rather light in the flavour department, this makes a MAJOR difference.

First you hollow the pumpkin out like was said before, but you DO NOT peel it.  Instead, slice the pumpkin into manageable chunks, and place them on a wire rack atop a shallow baking dish.  Put a couple cups of water in the bottom of the baking dish, and leave just a little space between the pumpkin on the wire rack, and the level of the water.  Then you will place this in the oven at 350 farenheit for between 45 minutes and 2 hours.  (It depends on your oven, and how much liquid there is in the pumpkin, and in the dish.)  

The result you're going for is that the skin of the pumpkin should bubble and lift from the flesh.  It will also darken, and just BEGIN to get a few tiny spots of crisp almost-burnt bits.  You do not want it to burn, but you do want it to roast for as long as possible, as this will make the rest of the processes much faster.

At that point, remove the pumpkin from the oven, and let it rest for a few minutes until it is still warm to the touch, but not so hot you'll burn yourself.  Then you'll use a sharp thin knife, like a pairing or fiilleting knife, and slive off all the skin, and any bits that are too dry, or dark.  THEN you can mash/strain everything OR if you don't want to deal with that?  Just throw it all into a food processor, which works just as well.

The additional time and effort brings a wonderful rich flavour to it that just doesn't exist otherwise.

Author: @alekssavic1154
Content: Re 11:10 ish: that's actually pretty common misunderstanding (unfortunately perpetuated by the "heritage minutes" on tv here in Canada); he actually did know it meant village. His writings refer the area around the St. Lawrence as "le pays du canadas" or "the country of villages" because there were no large cities but were many smaller settlements along the river (compared to other parts of the Atlantic coast which were much more sparsely populated). He says that's what he means explicitly at one point, but some historian later on missed that or didn't have access to the original text (I forget the exact details) and so interpreted "Le pays du canadas" literally and included that interpretation in a book which then spread it through Canadian academia. When the heritage minutes (for non-Canadians, the Canadian government at some point produced a series of short ads depicting certain important moments in Canadian history to run on TV during ad breaks) were being produced they unfortunately didn't do very thorough research so a few (fairly common) misconceptions found their way into those.

Content: I have heard that Cartier did not apply the word "Kanata" or Canada to the region in general (which he called New France) but did call the specific area of that village by that name. The extension of it to the greater area came after people knew that Canada meant village, and called the wider region that village was in "The Canadas" in other words, 'The Villages'. Author: @Psyche0delic
Content: You actually do not need to peel pumpkins if you are going to boil them until soft.  Just chop the pumpkin "meat" up into cubes, skin still left on, and boil.  The skin will become soft too and does not add a weird texture or subtract from the flavour.  This also works with other squash, like butternut, or whatever.  As an added bonus, you retain all of the nutrients that are present in the skin, making it healthier.  Peeling large squashes like a pumpkin is a royal pain, so skipping this step makes things A LOT easier and quicker.

Author: @celia5815
Content: Thank you for showcasing our gastronomy and it's history! Nowadays in France when we make soup, the bread is more often at the top of the soup than at the bottom. You can even put the slice of bread at the top, cover it with shredded cheese and let it grill in the oven, delicious.  Sometimes the bread is just toasted, rubbed with fresh garlic cut in half and cut into little croutons. Presenting the soup in the pumpkin's shell is mostly reserved for festive occasions. Some french names for different types of pumpkins (we call it " les courges"): "citrouille" is for the biggest variety, then "potiron" is smaller, then "potimarron" is even smaller with a thinner shell that you can cook and eat (personal favorite, it has a distinct nut-like after-taste). The white one we call it "patisson", it is a decoration but also good to eat. And of course the butternut. There are more, I let the french cooks and gardeners tell us more. Sorry for the essay, the french can become extremely chatty when talking about food!

A traditional soup of the Charentes region in western France is pumpkin and chestnut blanded together, with chestnut pieces for decoration.
Soupe is originally the bread you thicken a broth with, then the thickened broth itself took that name. It progressively extended to broths thickened with other starchy ingredients, like potatoes, legumes, cereals (often barley, but oats work nicely) or pasta, and pumpkin flesh fits that role perfectly. So it is still a soupe even without the sop.

Content:
"I am ready for autumn" he said in the middle of November. :D
By the way, if you have a high speed blender, don't toss the stringy bits of the pumpkin away! Separate them from the seeds, dry the seeds for later use, and churn the stringy bits at 10k+ revolutions per minute into a liquid. You can add this liquid back to the soup or use it later as part of a sauce, like for pasta.

When you have a bunch of pumpkin seeds collected, you can put them in the blender, add twice the volume of water and blend away. Then press the liquid through a nutmilk bag to filter the unsoluble bits of the seeds out. The resulting milk tastes fantastic, despite being kind of greenish, by itself. Or you use it instead of cow milk in your pumpkin soup. But this will make the soup taste even more pumpkiny.

Content: Just a little tip...  If you plan on mashing or puree any winter squash, this includes acorn squash, butternut squash, spaghetti squash, etc. any thick skinned squash, just split it in half, gut it, and place it in a glass baking dish cut side down. Author: @simonederobert1612
Content: For years I have been buying and using Pie Pumpkins, cooking (baking) them, then freezing some for later use. I have found that one Pie Pumpkin makes about 4 cups of shell-less pumpkin. My method of baking allows for the most useful amount of pumpkin. First: Preheat the oven to 350 F, then wash the fruit. Cut through the middle horizontally. One half will include the stem end, the other half includes the bottom end. Second: Scrape out all seeds and as much of the strings as you can. These can be washed and baked separately for snacking. Third: Place the cut pumpkin, cut sides down, on a baking tray/sheet, and bake for 50-60 minutes. Fourth: Allow to cool. The skin will peel off effortlessly, leaving the pulp ready to be used in whatever recipe you wish, only needing to be mashed. It may be necessary to thin with water or broth for easier soup or pie making. I have found this the easiest way to get to use Pie Pumpkin flesh without too much risk of cutting off my fingers, or stabbing myself with knife or peeler in order to get at the flesh.

Author: @elviejodelmar2795
Content:
Some history of the timetable of the pumpkin's trip, as part of the Three Sisters, from Oaxaca to those Huron and Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) lands in the north. In the Three Sisters, corn, beans, and squash are planted together. The corn provides a stalk for the beans to climb, beans fix nitrogen in the soil, and squash provides ground cover to retain moisture.
Mexico produced maize around 9,000 BCE, squash around 10,000 BCE, and beans between 2,000 and 1,500 BCE. The three-crop combination (The Three Sisters) emerged between 1,000 and 800 BCE.
Maize reached the Mississippi Valley and eastern woodlands by 200-300 BCE, but the Three Sisters didn't take hold until around 900-1000 CE.

Author: @nikkiewhite476
Content:
Fantastic video Max and thank you for the captions José! 
Pumpkins are such a versatile vegetable. My step-grandmother wrote her own cookbooks about pumpkin! She lived in Smokey lake Alberta and it holds one of the many pumpkin weigh-offs every fall. It was a serious competition in that town having many local people competing. 
Grandma wrote 2 cookbooks about pumpkin the second including zucchini recipes. She had everything from breads to entrees to desserts, she even had a way to make pumpkin liquor! She even had pumpkin pasta noodles. 
She sold the recipe books at the pumpkin faire every years. Until she retired in her late seventies. 
Pumpkin actually makes an excellent baby food. I made it for my son and pumpkin is still one of his favorite foods. 
He makes pumpkin and Leek soup with kabocha (often called Japanese pumpkin) quite often. It really is divine. 
Take care you two!

Author: @CourtneySchwartz
Content: Easier, more flavorful pumpkin purée: Slice in half (leave stem and skin).  Scoop out seeds with a spoon. Put face down into a crock or pan with about 250 mL/1 cup water to steam it. Bake at 190 C/375 F for 1 hour. Scoop softened flesh into blender. Add a little of the pumpkin water if needed. Flavor is richer, slightly caramelly, and the water-soluble vitamins like zinc are not boiled out. So much better than canned pumpkin that we’ve never gone back.
